title: Come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:6–21)
hookLine: the Bible ends with a prayer: even so, come, Lord Jesus

cards: Two voices, one after the other, in the second-to-last verse of a Christian Bible. The one who testifies to these things says, "Surely I come quickly."
And the answer comes straight back: "Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus." Then one line of blessing, and the book is closed.
After a garden, a flood, kings and exile, a cross and an empty tomb, beasts and a city of gold, the answer near the very end is one short word: come.
Today's word is an even older way of saying it, in a language that isn't Greek at all.

teach.b: First, the word. In the King James, maranatha turns up near the end of Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, left untranslated, in a hard line: "let him be Anathema Maranatha."
Paul writes in Greek, but this word is Aramaic, and he doesn't explain it, as if the church already knew it. Readers divide it two ways. Marana tha: our Lord, come.
Or maran atha: our Lord has come. A plea or a statement; the letters can carry both. Revelation's ending echoes the plea.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT AND THE BRIDE SAY COME.
teach.b: Second, everyone is saying it: "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come." The same word goes up to Christ and out to anyone thirsty. Third, quickly.
Christians have read it as soon in time, sudden when it happens, or simply certain. The book doesn't explain, and the church has kept saying come anyway. Fourth, where the word lives now.
Paul tells the Corinthians that when they eat the bread and drink the cup, they "shew the Lord's death till he come."

teach.h: KEPT AT A TABLE, ENDED IN GRACE.
teach.b: So the waiting is kept at a table. Some Christians say "come, Lord Jesus" in a grace before meals. Some churches sing maranatha in Advent, the weeks before Christmas.
And the very last verse of the Bible isn't a warning at all: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen."

how: Some Christians say 'come, Lord Jesus' in a grace before meals, and some churches sing or pray maranatha during Advent, the weeks of waiting before Christmas.

o: an Aramaic word: our Lord, come
a Greek warning: the end is near
a Hebrew blessing: peace be with you

games.q: the end of the book — tap the pairs.
p: said by the one who testifies

maranatha appears in one of Paul's letters, left untranslated
at the end of 1 Corinthians: "let him be Anathema Maranatha."
in Revelation 22 only the church says come
the Spirit and the bride say come, the one who hears says come, and the thirsty are told to come.

games.q: you're at the very end of the book. the voice says, "surely I come quickly." what comes back?
games.why: "Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus." the Bible's second-to-last verse is a short prayer: come.

practice: If you pray, let the old word ride on your breath in four even, unhurried syllables, ma-ra-na-tha, the way some Christian meditation groups say it, coming back to it whenever your mind wanders.
If you don't pray, sit with the plain English word come, and notice what you're waiting for: someone to arrive, something to mend, an ending to be good. Either way, don't hurry it.

wordCard.voice: Maranatha. An Aramaic word Paul left untranslated: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. At the end of Revelation: even so, come, Lord Jesus.

orig.note: Aramaic, written in Greek letters in 1 Corinthians 16:22: "our Lord, come" (or, divided differently, "our Lord has come").

carryVoice: Your line: come, Lord Jesus. Said by the Spirit, the bride, and anyone who's thirsty. See you tomorrow.
